newsReadings.title: Voyager 1 Reaches One Light-Day From Earth
newsReadings.source: Smithsonian Magazine, 18 November 2026; NASA Science, November 2026
newsReadings.passage:
On 18 November 2026, at 5:16 in the morning Eastern Standard Time, a spacecraft launched when disco dominated the charts crossed a boundary no human-made object had ever reached. At that moment, NASA's Voyager 1 stood one light-day from Earth — roughly 25.9 billion kilometres, or 16.1 billion miles, from the planet on which it was built. A radio signal travelling at the speed of light now needs a full 24 hours to make the journey, and any reply takes another day to come home. For the engineers who still tend the spacecraft, a simple question and its answer are now separated by two days.

A light-day is a measure of distance rather than time: the distance light covers in 24 hours. Put another way, Voyager 1 is now 173 times farther from the Sun than the Earth is, and more than four times as distant as Pluto. The milestone is, in NASA's own words, symbolic — the spacecraft detected no change in its surroundings as it crossed the threshold — yet it captures something remarkable about endurance. Voyager 1 was launched on 5 September 1977, sixteen days after its identical twin, Voyager 2, on a mission originally intended to last only a few years and to study Jupiter and Saturn. Nearly half a century later, it is still transmitting, still navigating interstellar space, and still, in a limited sense, answering commands.

The journey has been one of steady improvisation. In August 2012, Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause, the boundary where the Sun's influence gives way to the space between the stars, becoming the first human-made object to enter interstellar space. It now travels at about 38,000 miles per hour relative to the Sun — roughly 17 kilometres every second — in the direction of a star known as Gliese 445, which it will pass within about 1.6 light-years in some 40,000 years. Its twin, Voyager 2, is not expected to reach the one-light-day mark until November 2035.

Keeping the spacecraft alive has become an exercise in careful rationing. Its electricity comes from plutonium-238, a power source whose output declines by about four watts each year. To conserve what remains, mission controllers have switched off instruments one by one. According to an update in April 2026, only two of the original ten science instruments were still operating: the magnetometer, which measures magnetic fields, and the plasma wave subsystem, which studies charged particles. The cosmic ray and low-energy charged particle instruments had been switched off to save power, a decision that trades scientific breadth for longevity.

The growing distance compounds every difficulty. Commands that once arrived in hours now take a day, so engineers must plan each instruction with unusual care; there is no opportunity to correct a mistake quickly. The signal itself, weakened by the vast distance, must be caught by the giant antennas of NASA's Deep Space Network, and even then the data trickle home at a rate far slower than a household internet connection. Yet the team has repeatedly found ways to keep the mission going, reviving thrusters and reworking software from billions of kilometres away.

NASA marked the occasion with public events on both sides of the milestone, including a global "Shine Bright" moment on 17 November and a discussion with mission scientists on 19 November. The timing also looks ahead: in the summer of 2027, Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 will each reach fifty years in space. Whether Voyager 1 is still sending data by then depends on the slow arithmetic of its fading power supply. What is already certain is that no other object built by human hands has travelled so far, and that the faint signal still arriving each day is, in effect, a message from a machine that has outlived every expectation placed upon it.

questions.q: What did Voyager 1 achieve on 18 November 2026?
options: It became the first human-made object to reach one light-day from Earth.
It landed on the surface of a distant star.
It completed fifty years in space.
It sent back the first photograph of interstellar space.

questions.q: How long does a radio signal now take to travel one way between Earth and Voyager 1?
Why have mission controllers switched off several of Voyager 1's instruments?
options: The instruments were damaged during launch.
To conserve the spacecraft's declining power supply.
NASA ordered the mission to end in 2026.
The instruments had completed all their scientific work.

All ten of Voyager 1's original science instruments are still operating.
Voyager 1 will pass within about 1.6 light-years of the star Gliese 445 in around 40,000 years.

newsReadings.title: COP31: From Climate Promises to Practice
newsReadings.passage:
The United Nations climate conference known as COP31 opened in Antalya, Türkiye, on 9 November 2026 with a question that has haunted climate diplomacy for a decade: how do countries turn promises into practice? For two weeks, until 20 November, negotiators are wrestling less with new targets than with implementation — the unglamorous work of putting existing commitments into effect. Electrification, carbon markets, adaptation finance and international cooperation dominate the agenda, and a strengthening El Niño, which can disrupt weather patterns worldwide, has added urgency to preparations for climate impacts that are already arriving.

At the centre of the implementation debate is carbon pricing: the idea that emitting greenhouse gases should carry a cost, encouraging businesses and governments to choose cleaner alternatives. The European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, or CBAM, is the most ambitious attempt to put that principle into practice across borders. It charges a levy on certain carbon-intensive goods imported into the EU, based on the emissions produced in making them, so that European manufacturers are not undercut by competitors operating under weaker climate rules. On 18 November, the European Commission announced that the mechanism's area would be extended to Iceland and Norway, following a decision by the EEA Joint Committee that entered into force the same day. From 1 January 2027, the mechanism will apply in full to goods entering the customs territories of the two countries, just as it does to goods entering the EU.

Supporters argue that the extension shows carbon pricing can spread beyond the bloc that invented it, creating a wider zone in which polluting carries a price. Critics, however, warn that border levies risk becoming a new source of trade friction, particularly for developing economies whose industries cannot yet afford the transition. That tension was audible in Antalya, where India called for equity, climate justice and the fulfilment of climate finance obligations — a reminder that the countries most exposed to climate damage are often those that contributed least to causing it. India also pointed to its own progress: its total installed renewable energy capacity stood at 299.25 gigawatts by September 2026, evidence, its delegation argued, that large developing economies can expand clean energy rapidly when investment flows.

Adaptation finance — money to help vulnerable countries cope with floods, droughts and rising seas — remains one of the most contested issues at the conference. Delegates from small island states and the least developed countries have long argued that funding for adaptation lags far behind funding for cutting emissions, even though the two are inseparable: a sea wall and a solar panel address different halves of the same crisis. The strengthening El Niño sharpens the argument, since the phenomenon is associated with heavier rainfall in some regions and drought in others, testing infrastructure and food systems that are already under strain.

What makes COP31 different from earlier summits is the shift in emphasis from pledging to delivering. Previous conferences produced a thicket of targets and timetables; Antalya is, by design, a test of whether the machinery built to meet them actually works. Carbon pricing schemes must be administered fairly, finance must reach the places that need it, and national plans must be translated into power plants built, grids upgraded and homes protected. The conference will be judged not by the ambition of its final text alone, but by whether the mechanisms it strengthens — from border adjustments to adaptation funds — begin to function in the months that follow. For the delegates in Antalya, the distance between a promise and a result is now the whole of the task. If the fortnight ends with working systems rather than fresh slogans, it will have earned its place as the conference where climate diplomacy finally started to deliver.

questions.q: What is the main focus of COP31 in Antalya, according to the passage?
options: Setting new global temperature targets for the first time.
Turning existing climate commitments into practical action.
Banning all fossil fuel production immediately.
Moving the conference to a different country each year.

questions.q: What change to the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism was announced on 18 November?
options: It was abolished by the European Commission.
It was extended to Iceland and Norway from 1 January 2027.
It was replaced by a global carbon tax.
It was limited to goods made inside the EU only.

questions.q: Why does the passage mention a strengthening El Niño?
options: It has ended all droughts in affected regions.
It adds urgency to preparing for climate impacts.
It proves that carbon pricing does not work.
It caused COP31 to be postponed.

questions.q: COP31 is being held in Antalya, Türkiye, from 9 to 20 November 2026.
The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism already applied to Iceland and Norway before 2027.
India's total installed renewable energy capacity stood at 299.25 gigawatts by September 2026.
All countries at COP31 agreed a new binding global emissions target.
